symptoms: Brown leaf spots that may develop concentric rings; lesions can also appear on stems and fruit. Symptoms often begin on older or lower foliage.
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen; the reviewed source gives no fertilizer cure.
treatment: ICAR advises copper oxychloride or a registered metalaxyl+mancozeb product when symptoms appear. Remove severely affected lower leaves and seek local confirmation if uncertain.
dosage: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisory 2025 gives copper oxychloride 3 g/L or metalaxyl 4% + mancozeb 64% WP 1.5 g/L for its advisory context. Confirm the exact formulation, current registration, crop label and pre-harvest interval before use.
safety_note: Use only products currently registered for tomato and the named disease; follow the product label, PPE, re-entry interval and pre-harvest interval. Do not mix products unless the label allows it.

symptoms: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the blossom end of the fruit.
cause: Often associated with inconsistent soil moisture and calcium delivery; symptoms alone do not confirm a soil calcium deficiency.
fertilizer: The reviewed ICAR advisory mentions calcium chloride foliar application in affected areas; assess irrigation and soil conditions first.
treatment: Keep soil moisture more even and avoid large swings in watering. Confirm the diagnosis locally, since similar fruit damage can have other causes.
dosage: The ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisory 2025 states calcium chloride 5 g/L foliar application in its advisory context. Check local guidance and the product label before applying.
safety_note: Do not assume every dark fruit lesion is calcium deficiency. Follow the product label and local horticulture/KVK advice.

symptoms: Early blight lesions on leaves, stems or fruit; leaf lesions can show characteristic concentric markings.
fertilizer: No fertilizer recommendation in this source.
treatment: Use integrated disease-management guidance and confirm the diagnosis before choosing a fungicide.
dosage: No spray dosage included in this source entry; consult a current local recommendation and the registered product label.
safety_note: Do not diagnose from one symptom alone; seek a local agricultural expert for uncertain cases.

symptoms: Leaves curl or deform, leaves become small, internodes shorten and plants become stunted; flower buds may drop.
cause: Viral disease commonly transmitted by whiteflies; similar symptoms can have other causes.
fertilizer: No fertilizer cures a viral infection.
treatment: Use healthy, disease-free seed and nursery protection; remove severely infected plants to reduce sources of infection and manage the vector using current local integrated pest-management advice.
dosage: No pesticide dosage included; consult a local KVK/agricultural officer and use only currently registered products according to their labels.
safety_note: The source says control measures are not known for many viral diseases. Do not claim an insecticide cures infected plants.

symptoms: Small bluish-green flecks enlarge into spindle-shaped leaf spots with grey centres and dark-brown margins; black lesions can girdle nodes, and neck lesions can cause panicles to fall.
cause: Magnaporthe oryzae (synonyms in the source include Pyricularia grisea and Magnaporthe grisea).
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen; follow a soil-test-based, locally recommended nutrient plan.
treatment: Use an integrated, locally recommended disease-management plan; confirm symptoms and crop stage with a local agricultural expert.
dosage: No chemical dosage included in this entry; check the latest local advisory and the registered product label.
safety_note: Advisories vary by region, cultivar and crop stage. Observe label precautions and pre-harvest intervals.

symptoms: Yellowing followed by wilting, often in patches; leaves may roll upward and inward and remain attached after wilting.
fertilizer: No fertilizer cure is stated in this source.
treatment: TNAU recommends resistant varieties and describes seed treatment and biological/cultural management options. Confirm diagnosis and locally suitable treatment with an expert.
dosage: No field spray dosage included in this entry; follow current local recommendations and product labels.
safety_note: Wilt symptoms overlap across diseases. Do not apply pesticides based only on visual symptoms.

symptoms: Older leaves turn yellowish green; shoots grow slowly and plants look spindly or pale. Severe deficiency can make the whole plant pale.
cause: Nitrogen deficiency is a possible cause; other stresses can produce similar symptoms.
fertilizer: Urea is a nitrogen fertilizer; confirm nutrient deficiency and local suitability before application.
treatment: TNAU describes foliar urea for nitrogen deficiency. Obtain soil or tissue testing and local agricultural advice before choosing treatment.
dosage: TNAU lists a 1% foliar urea spray twice at weekly intervals in its advisory. Confirm product suitability and local recommendations before use.
safety_note: Yellow leaves alone do not confirm nitrogen deficiency. Avoid excess nitrogen and follow product labels and local expert advice.

symptoms: Older leaves turn yellow between veins, beginning near the margins; affected areas can become brown and withered.
cause: Magnesium deficiency is a possible cause; similar yellowing has other causes.
fertilizer: Magnesium sulphate supplies magnesium; soil amendments should be chosen after local soil assessment.
treatment: TNAU describes foliar magnesium sulphate or a soil application. Confirm the deficiency with soil or tissue testing and local advice.
dosage: TNAU lists 2% magnesium sulphate foliar spray twice at fortnightly intervals, or soil application options. Confirm local suitability and product label before use.
safety_note: Symptoms alone do not confirm a deficiency; a soil or tissue test and local guidance help prevent inappropriate applications.
